explication:
<explanation>
1. Project Type & Purpose  
   - Woodpecker is a full-stack, extensible CI/CD engine written in Go, composed of a server (API, business logic, persistence, queueing, pub/sub), an agent for executing pipeline steps on various backends, a CLI for scripting/automation, and a web UI for human interaction.  

2. High-Level File Structure Analysis  
   - Top-level “cmd/…” folders: entry points for `woodpecker-server`, `woodpecker-agent`, `woodpecker-cli`.  
   - `server/`: REST & gRPC API handlers, router, services layer, store (database + migrations), pub/sub, queue, cron scheduler, model definitions.  
   - `agent/`: gRPC client, pipeline runner, tracer, state management.  
   - `cli/`: commands for admin/org/repo/pipeline management, setup, linting, execution, update.  
   - `pipeline/`: core pipeline library (frontend YAML compiler & linter → DAG → types → backend executors for Docker/Kubernetes/local/dummy) plus logging, tracer, RPC definitions.  
   - `web/`: Vue.js single-page app consuming server’s REST API.  
   - `shared/`, `woodpecker-go/`: shared utilities and Go client libraries.  

3. README Insights  
   - CI/CD engine runs with SQLite by default (configurable).  
   - Components interact over REST, gRPC, and pub/sub.  
   - Agents connect to server for work via gRPC.  
   - Supports plugins, multiple SCM forges, extensible backends.  

4. Creating the System Design Diagram  
   a. Main Components  
      - Client Tier:  
        • Web UI (Vue.js SPA)  
        • CLI (Go binary)  
        • woodpecker-go client library  
      - Server Tier:  
        • API Gateway (HTTP + gRPC endpoints in `server/api` & `server/grpc`)  
        • Business Services (configuration, encryption, environment, permissions, registry, secret)  
        • Queue & Pub/Sub (in-memory or persistent FIFO queue, pub/sub topic for logs/events)  
        • Scheduler/Cron subsystem  
        • Pipeline Orchestrator (`server/pipeline`, sharing core with `pipeline/`)  
      - Data Tier:  
        • Relational DB via `server/store/datastore` (SQLite, MySQL, Postgres) + migrations  
      - Execution Tier:  
        • Agent(s) (gRPC clients under `agent/`)  
        • Pipeline Backend Executors (Docker, Kubernetes, Local, Dummy under `pipeline/backend`)  
      - External Services:  
        • SCM Forge Webhooks (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea, etc. via `server/forge/*`)  
        • Metrics/Monitoring (Prometheus endpoint)  
        • Container Registry integration  
        • Plugin registry (optional)  

   b. Relationships & Data Flows  
      - User → Web UI / CLI calls → Server API  
      - Server API → Services → Store (DB reads/writes)  
      - Server enqueues pipeline jobs → Queue → Agent polls  
      - Agent fetches job → runs via pipeline/backend → streams logs back → Server pub/sub → stored + forwarded to UI/CLI  
      - SCM webhook → Server API webhook handler → triggers pipeline creation  
      - Cron scheduler in server → enqueues scheduled pipeline jobs  
      - Metrics server exposes Prometheus metrics  

   c. Architectural Patterns & Principles  
      - Layered Architecture: API → Services → Store  
      - Event-Driven through Queue & Pub/Sub  
      - Plugin-Based Extensibility in pipeline backends and server forges  
      - Shared library (`pipeline/`) for core pipeline logic used by server and agent  
      - Micro-services boundary between Server and Agent via gRPC  

   d. Key Technologies & Frameworks  
      - Go language, gRPC, Protobuf  
      - HTTP router & middleware (`server/router`)  
      - XORM for DB migrations (`server/store/datastore/xorm.go`)  
      - Vue.js + Vite for Web UI  
      - Cobra/Viper (implied in CLI flags/config)  
      - Docker/Kubernetes clients in pipeline backend  

5. Tailoring the Diagram for Woodpecker  
   - Emphasize separation of concerns:  
     • Frontend layer (Web UI) vs. CLI vs. API Gateway  
     • Orchestrator vs. Execution agents  
     • Persistence vs. messaging vs. compute  
   - Show shared pipeline library used by both server (to compile schedules, validate) and agent (to execute).  
   - Highlight plugin/forge integrations as pluggable modules.  

6. Diagramming Guidelines  
   - Use clear rectangular boxes for each component group (e.g., UI, API, Services, Store, Agent, External).  
   - Draw directional arrows:  
     • API calls (Web UI/CLI → Server API)  
     • Data flows (Server → DB, Server ↔ Queue, Queue → Agent)  
     • Control flows (SCM Webhook → Server)  
   - Color-code:  
     • Blue for client-side (Web, CLI),  
     • Green for server internals (API, Services),  
     • Orange for data/persistence (DB, Queue, Pub/Sub),  
     • Purple for execution (Agent, Pipeline Backend),  
     • Gray for external systems (SCM, Metrics).  
   - Label protocols on arrows (HTTP, gRPC, SQL, Pub/Sub).  
   - Group related modules in swimlanes or containers (e.g., “Server Process” containing API, Services, Store).  

7. Level of Detail  
   - Capture all essential modules: router/middleware, API endpoints, business services, store layers, queue/pubsub, cron scheduler, pipeline orchestrator, agent RPC, pipeline backends.  
   - Don’t over-complicate: show module clusters rather than every single package.  
   - Ensure each arrow and label conveys purpose—trigger, request, job dispatch, log stream, data store.  
   - Include a legend explaining shapes and colors.  
   - Review existing `docs/docs/92-development/05-architecture.md` and `architecture.excalidraw` for inspiration and to ensure consistency with project documentation.  
</explanation>
